title: The Principle of Rebirth
author: Zhanran
excerpt: The principle of rebirth: right mindfulness at the moment of death, which invites the Buddha's coming to welcome.

inline.s: The principle of rebirth: right mindfulness at the moment of death, which invites the Buddha's coming to welcome.
Q: What is the principle of rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss?
Answer: The principle of rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss is:
right mindfulness at death, which invites the Buddha's coming to welcome.
Master Lianchi (Zhuhong) says:
“Within, focus the mind on right mindfulness; without, sense the Buddha's coming to welcome.”
(from the Commentary on the Amitabha Sutra)
[Right mindfulness at death, inviting the Buddha's coming to welcome] At the moment of death, maintain
the Buddha-recitation's
right mindfulness, and be in mutual resonance (gǎnyìng) with the Buddha, so that the Buddha comes to receive and guide. Therefore Master Shandao, the manifestation of Amitabha Buddha, instructs:
“When it is sustained, one is reborn”
(at death, so long as one's Buddha-recitation thought is sustained without being cut off by stray thoughts, one is reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss)
Both Master Tanluan and Master Daochuo instruct:
if the ten recitations at death are sustained, one will be reborn.
(For details see
Master Shandao's Pure Land Teachings
Master Tanluan's Pure Land Teachings
, and
Master Daochuo's Pure Practice Teachings

As for the case of those who at death are upside-down, without right mindfulness, and who, drawn along by the force of karma, are reborn in the corresponding destiny among the six paths (rebirth in accord with karma),
Master Lianchi
instructs

“Those who are upside-down at death — because they used to follow after deluded thoughts and did not cultivate right mindfulness, their minds were scattered. At the moment of leaving the warm touch (of the body), all the deeds of a lifetime appear before them, and their spirits are terrified and their movements wild. Those who should enter hell see the mountain of knives and the forest of swords as a garden. Those who should fall among animals take the womb of a horse or the belly of a donkey as a palace. Even those who have done good and should be born among humans or gods cannot help loving and hating their parents. Even lesser sages at their initial resolve cannot rightly know their entering and leaving. All these are what are called being upside-down. Through this upside-down state, within the three realms and the seven destinies,
they are reborn according to karma
(from the Commentary on the Amitabha Sutra)

Translation: Those who are upside-down at death, because they used to follow after deluded thoughts and did not cultivate right mindfulness, have scattered minds. When the four great elements dissolve, all the deeds of a lifetime appear before them, their spirits are terrified, and their movements are confounded. Those who should enter hell take the mountain of knives and the forest of swords to be a beautiful garden. Those who should fall among animals take the womb of a horse and the belly of a donkey to be a splendid hall. Even those who have done good and should be born in the human or heavenly path, upon entering the womb, cannot help loving the mother and hating the father to be born male, or loving the father and hating the mother to be born female. Even the lesser sages of the first stage (of the Śrāvaka path) and bodhisattvas of initial resolve still have the delusion of the intervening birth (géyīn zhī mí) and cannot rightly know entering and leaving the womb. These are all the so-called upside-down states. Through this upside-down state at death, in the seven destinies within the three realms, they are reborn according to karma.
[Seven destinies] Hell, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, spirit immortals, gods, and asuras. “Destiny” (qù) means a going, a direction.
The Zhongfeng Three-Fold Contemplation (Zhongfeng Sanshi Xinian) says:

“Yet although it is said that Amitabha gathers in sentient beings for rebirth, one must believe that it is only manifested in accord with one's own mind, an interpenetration of response and resonance; ultimately it is not obtained from without.”

[Only manifested in accord with one's own mind] The minds of sentient beings are like water; Amitabha Buddha is like the moon. When the water of the mind is clear (still and clear), the Buddha-moon appears; when the water of the mind is stirred and muddy (in motion and muddy), though the Buddha-moon shines, its reflection is not clearly seen. [Interpenetration of response and resonance] The response (the sense) of sentient beings and the resonance (the response) of Amitabha Buddha interpenetrate each other.
Master Yinguang, speaking of the principle of mutual resonance at the time of death, says:

“The minds of sentient beings are like water; Amitabha Buddha is like the moon. When sentient beings have complete faith and vows and sincerely sense the Buddha, the Buddha responds, as when the water is clear the moon appears. If the mind is not pure and sincere, and accords with greed, anger, and delusion, turning away from the Buddha, it is like water that is muddy and moving; though the moon does not fail to shine upon it, its reflection cannot be clearly manifested.”
(from Master Yinguang's Collected Writings,
Preface to the Guide to Pure Karma for Beginners)

This says: The minds of sentient beings are like pools of water; Amitabha Buddha is like the bright moon in the sky. When sentient beings at death sense the Buddha with right mindfulness, the Buddha responds; if the pool of water is clear and still, the bright moon's reflection appears within it. This is a metaphor: right mindfulness at death senses and manifests Amitabha Buddha's coming to welcome. If at the moment of death the mind is not pure, not sincere, accords with greed, anger, and delusion, and turns away from the Buddha, it is like a pool of muddy, agitated water; though the bright moon in the sky does not fail to shine upon it, the moon cannot be clearly reflected in that pool. This is a metaphor: an agitated, muddy, deluded mind at death cannot sense and manifest Amitabha Buddha's coming to receive and guide.
Concerning
the single thought conditioned at death
, Master Chewu instructs:
[The single thought conditioned at death] The thought, at the moment of death, that determines where the consciousness (shénshí) goes to be reborn.

“Our present single thought is conditioned and without self-nature, and without self-nature it is conditioned. If one does not give birth to the Buddha-realm, one gives birth to one of the nine realms. If we take it as conditioned and without self-nature, then sentient beings and Buddha are equally one emptiness. If we take it as without self-nature and conditioned, then the ten realms differ vastly in excellence and inferiority. King Aśoka, at his death, because a fly-whisking servant brushed his face with a whisk, gave rise to a single thought of anger and fell to become a venomous snake. A woman fording a river slipped, and her child fell into the water; because she reached for the child, she sank with it. Because of her mind of compassion, she was reborn in heaven. Since a single thought of compassion or anger at once divides heaven from the animals, should one not be careful with this single thought conditioned at death? If with this mind one turns to the thought of Amitabha and seeks rebirth in the Pure Land, how could one fail to see the Buddha and be reborn?”

Translation: Our present single thought is conditioned and without self-nature; without self-nature it is conditioned. If one does not give birth to the Buddha-realm, one gives birth to one of the nine realms. If we take it as conditioned and without self-nature, then sentient beings and the Buddha are equal, both being one emptiness. If we take it as without self-nature and conditioned, then among the ten realms the excellence or inferiority is very vast. When King Aśoka was dying, a fly-whisking servant happened to brush his face with a fan, and a single thought of anger arose; because this dying thought was one of anger, he fell to become a venomous snake. A woman fording a river slipped, and her child fell into the water; because she went to save the child, both she and the child were drowned. Because her dying thought was one of compassion, this woman was reborn in heaven. A dying thought of compassion or anger — the compassionate one is born in heaven, the angry one is born an animal, so that excellence and inferiority are at once divided — how can one fail to be cautious with this single dying thought conditioned at death? If at death with this mind one turns to the thought of Amitabha and seeks rebirth in the Pure Land, how could one fail to see the Buddha and be reborn?

[Without self-nature] “Dharmas have no self-nature” means that all dharmas have no real substance; they are all illusions, like things in a dream. Without self-nature is also called no-nature. The Treatise on Consciousness-Only says: “All dharmas are without self-nature.” The Lotus Sutra says: “Know that dharmas are ever without self-nature.” The Surangama Sutra says: “All illusions become without self-nature.” [Nine realms] Among the ten realms, the other nine besides the Buddha-realm. [Ten realms] Hell, hungry ghosts, animals, asuras, humans, gods, Śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and Buddha. The first six are the six ordinary states; the last four are the four sages. [King Aśoka] King Aśoka (Aqídá wáng), who in his life built countless stupas, made offerings to the Three Jewels, upheld the true Dharma, and had vast merit. At the moment of death, because his attendant carelessly brushed his face with a fan, he gave rise to a thought of anger and fell to become a venomous snake. The matter appears in the Scripture of Miscellaneous Parables.

“But this single thought cannot be had by mere luck. One must hold it with sincerity and maintain it through constant practice. Therefore we who practice this single phrase Amitabha, reciting it a thousand times and ten thousand times, even all day and all year, do so only to mature this single thought. If one single thought is fully matured, then at the moment of death there is only this thought, with no other thought besides. Master Zhiyi says: ‘The mind that is in concentration at death is the mind that is reborn in the Pure Land.’ Now if there is only this thought and no other thought, is it not the mind in concentration? If the thought is truly so, and one does not see Amitabha, whom else would one see? If one is not reborn in the Pure Land, where else would one be reborn? I only fear that we do not have enough faith in ourselves.
(from the Collected Works of Master Chewu)

Translation: But this single dying thought cannot be had by mere luck. One must hold it with sincerity and maintain it through constant practice. Therefore we, practicing this single phrase Amitabha, reciting it a thousand times, ten thousand times, even all day and all year, do so only to mature this single thought of Buddha-recitation, so as to ensure that the dying thought is one of reciting Amitabha. If the single thought of Buddha-recitation is truly fully matured, then at the moment of death there is only this thought of Buddha-recitation, with no other thought. Master Zhiyi says: ‘The mind in concentration at death is the mind that is reborn in the Pure Land.’ If there is only the thought of Buddha-recitation and no other thought, is that not a mind in concentration? Since at death one is in a mind of concentration, if one does not see Amitabha, whom else would one see? If one is not reborn in the Pure Land, where else would one be reborn? I only fear that we have not truly believed in the principle above. If we truly believed, how could we fail to strive to mature this single thought of Buddha-recitation and be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss?

[To mature this single thought] One must achieve what Mahasthamaprapta calls “pure thought continuing unbroken,” which is also what Master Shandao (the second Patriarch of the Pure Land school) calls “thought after thought sustained.” (Note: “thought after thought sustained” means the thought of Buddha-recitation sustained from one thought to the next, not the case of reciting Amitabha aloud with the mouth while the mind wanders in delusion.) Master Shandao says: “Therefore the Great Sage (Śākyamuni Buddha), with compassion, directly urges exclusive recitation of the Name; precisely because the recitation of the Name is easy, when it is sustained one is reborn. If one can sustain it thought after thought for the whole of life till death, then ten out of ten are reborn, a hundred out of a hundred are reborn. … I wish that all people would think this over well: whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying, they must rouse their minds and restrain themselves, not letting up by day or night; the last thought at the end of life, and the next thought, is reborn; forever enjoying the bliss of the unconditioned Dharma, up to the attainment of Buddhahood — how delightful!”
(For details see
Master Shandao's Pure Land Teachings
So, sustaining the thought day after day is the guarantee of clear right mindfulness at death; and clear right mindfulness at death is the key to rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.

Of the principle of resonance in “at death, within focus the mind on right mindfulness, without sense the Buddha's coming to welcome,” Master Yinguang has an incisive passage in his Preface to the Guide to Pure Karma for Beginners, which I now transcribe and annotate below:

“Someone says: Amitabha Buddha dwells at ease in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. The worlds of the ten directions are immeasurable and boundless. The sentient beings who recite the Buddha's name in a single world are likewise immeasurable and boundless. How can Amitabha Buddha, with one body, at one time universally receive and guide all the reciting sentient beings of the immeasurable and boundless worlds of the ten directions?”

Someone asks: Amitabha Buddha dwells at ease in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Yet the worlds of the ten directions are immeasurable and boundless, and the sentient beings who recite the Buddha's name in a single world are likewise immeasurable and boundless. How can Amitabha Buddha, with this one body, in a single moment, universally receive and guide all the reciting sentient beings of the immeasurable and boundless worlds of the ten directions?

“Answer: How can you, with the views of an ordinary man, speculate on the realm of the Buddha? Let me use a simile to make it clear and dispel your doubt. A single moon shines in the sky, and its reflection appears in ten thousand streams — does the moon take any thought to do so?”

Answer: How can you, with the views of an ordinary man, speculate on the realm of the Buddha? (The frog at the bottom of a well — how can it know there are still mountains, rivers, oceans, and towns?) Let me use a simile to explain and rid you of your doubt. A single bright moon hangs high in the sky, and its reflection appears in ten thousand rivers and streams — yet does the bright moon deliberately shine on this river or that?

“Now in the sky there is only one moon, and yet the great sea, the great rivers, the great streams, and the small brooks all reflect the full moon. Even in so small a thing as a single ladle or a drop of water, the full moon is always reflected in full.”

In the sky there is only one moon, and yet the great sea, the great rivers, the great streams, and the small brooks all reflect the full moon. Even down to a ladle or a drop of water, in each the full moon is reflected in full.

“… Only when the water is clear and still does it appear; when the water is muddy and moving it is hidden. The moon itself has no choosing and rejecting; where it does not appear, it is because the water is dim, muddy, and rushing, and so unable to receive its reflection.”

… However, only when the water is clear and still does the moon appear; when the water is muddy and moving, the moon is hidden. The moon indeed has no choosing or rejecting (the bright moon does not deliberately shine on some waters and not on others); where it does not appear, it is because the water is dim, muddy, and rushing, unable to receive its reflection. (So where a moon-reflection does not appear in some water, the fault lies not with the moon [“that land does not turn away”] but with the water [“it is drawn by its own nature”]. The Sukhāvatīvyūha Sutra, the Sutra of Amitāyus (Foshuo Wuliangshou Jing), says: “Rising to the Way is without limit or end, easy to go to, yet no one goes; that land does not turn away, but [sentient beings] are drawn by their own nature.”)
